title: DIAGNOSTIC ALGORITHM AND TREATMENT FOR MICROSCOPIC COLITIS: A REVIEW.

subsections.content:
The diagnostic framework for microscopic colitis (MC) begins with clinical suspicion in patients presenting with chronic or recurrent watery, nonbloody diarrhea, particularly older adults and women, often accompanied by urgency, nocturnal stools, abdominal pain, weight loss, or fecal incontinence. Because the endoscopic appearance is typically normal or only minimally abnormal, MC should be actively considered during the workup of chronic diarrhea even when colonoscopy is macroscopically unremarkable ref [1], ref [2].

Initial clinical workup should exclude more common or overlapping causes of chronic diarrhea, including celiac disease, bile acid diarrhea, medication-related diarrhea, infectious etiologies, and inflammatory bowel disease. A careful drug history is essential, given reported associations with proton-pump inhibitors, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors; evaluation for concomitant autoimmune disease is also warranted, particularly celiac disease and thyroid disorders ref [1], ref [2]. Routine laboratory testing is mainly supportive rather than diagnostic, and MC cannot be confirmed on symptoms or blood tests alone.

Definitive diagnosis requires colonoscopy with systematic colonic biopsies, including samples from the proximal and distal colon, since histologic abnormalities may be patchy and a rectosigmoid-only strategy can miss cases. The diagnosis is then classified histologically as collagenous colitis or lymphocytic colitis on the basis of characteristic mucosal inflammatory changes despite a grossly normal colon ref [1], ref [2]. Thus, the core diagnostic algorithm is a clinicopathologic one: suspect MC in chronic watery diarrhea, exclude major mimics, and confirm the diagnosis through adequate histopathologic sampling.

Fecal biomarkers have been investigated primarily as noninvasive tools to distinguish microscopic colitis (MC) from functional diarrhea and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), particularly because endoscopic appearance is often normal and definitive diagnosis still depends on histology. Current evidence indicates that fecal calprotectin (FC) is the most studied marker, but its diagnostic performance in MC is modest and appears to be most informative in active rather than quiescent disease. A major limitation is that FC levels in MC are generally lower than those typically observed in classical inflammatory bowel disease, which restricts its value as a standalone rule-in or rule-out test ref [3].

In a prospective study comparing MC and IBS, ELISA-based FC measurement was significantly higher in active MC than in IBS, whereas patients with MC in remission showed values closer to IBS controls. Notably, the rapid FC assay failed to detect this difference, underscoring that assay platform and analytical sensitivity materially affect clinical utility ref [4]. Thus, when chronic watery diarrhea raises a differential diagnosis between MC and IBS, a mildly elevated FC may support prioritizing colonoscopic biopsy, but a normal FC does not exclude MC ref [3], ref [4].

Other fecal inflammatory markers, including lactoferrin and eosinophil-derived proteins, have been explored, but available data remain inconsistent and insufficient for routine differential diagnosis. Overall, fecal biomarkers should be viewed as adjuncts within the diagnostic workup: they may help identify patients more likely to harbor organic mucosal inflammation, yet they cannot replace histopathologic confirmation or reliably subtype disease into collagenous versus lymphocytic colitis ref [3].

Eosinophil-associated fecal biomarkers are of particular interest in microscopic colitis because collagenous colitis appears to exhibit a more prominent eosinophil-driven inflammatory signature than a neutrophil-dominant one. In a pilot treatment study, fecal eosinophil cationic protein (F-ECP) showed the strongest ability to identify active collagenous colitis, with most patients demonstrating elevated baseline levels; fecal eosinophil protein X (F-EPX) was also frequently increased, whereas neutrophil-derived markers were less consistently informative ref [6]. These observations support the concept that eosinophil degranulation reflects biologically relevant mucosal activity rather than nonspecific diarrhea alone.

The diagnostic relevance of this pathway was further strengthened in patients undergoing colonoscopy for chronic non-bloody diarrhea, where elevated fecal eosinophil granule proteins predicted collagenous colitis ref [5]. This is clinically important because microscopic colitis often presents with symptoms overlapping irritable bowel syndrome, yet eosinophil-derived fecal proteins may better capture the characteristic inflammatory milieu than conventional inflammatory markers. Accordingly, eosinophil-associated assays may serve as adjunctive tools for selecting patients who warrant histologic evaluation, although they do not replace colonoscopic biopsy-based diagnosis.

Eosinophil biomarkers may also provide a dynamic measure of disease activity and treatment response. During budesonide therapy, F-ECP and F-EPX declined rapidly—within days in many cases—and normalized in most patients who entered clinical remission ref [6]. Thus, while current evidence remains limited and largely focused on collagenous colitis rather than lymphocytic colitis, eosinophil-associated fecal markers are among the most promising candidates for monitoring active disease and early therapeutic response in microscopic colitis.

subsections.subsection_title: Histologic and Immune Correlates Relevant to Diagnosis
subsections.content:
Histologic confirmation remains the diagnostic cornerstone in microscopic colitis because endoscopic appearances are often normal or only subtly abnormal. The two canonical patterns are a thickened subepithelial collagen band in collagenous colitis and prominent intraepithelial lymphocytosis in lymphocytic colitis, both typically accompanied by a chronic inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria. These tissue-level features are particularly important for distinguishing microscopic colitis from functional diarrhea and irritable bowel syndrome, as well as from other inflammatory disorders with overlapping symptoms.

Beyond routine histopathology, immune-cell profiling helps clarify diagnostically relevant inflammatory signatures. In collagenous colitis, colonic biopsies demonstrate increased eosinophils and T-cell populations, supporting the concept that the disorder reflects a mucosal immune activation rather than a nonspecific diarrheal state. Notably, flow-cytometric analysis has shown activated eosinophils in active collagenous colitis, whereas neutrophil activation is not a defining feature; this distinction is useful because it aligns microscopic colitis more closely with chronic lymphocytic-eosinophilic inflammation than with acute neutrophil-predominant colitis ref [7].

These immune correlates also have interpretive value when linked to treatment response. In active collagenous colitis, CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell numbers are increased, although their activation phenotype may differ from that seen in controls, and budesonide-induced remission is accompanied by normalization of eosinophil and T-cell activity ref [7]. Accordingly, while histology remains the primary diagnostic standard, integration of structural findings with mucosal immune signatures may improve diagnostic confidence, help explain clinicopathologic heterogeneity, and provide a biologic framework for differentiating microscopic colitis from other chronic diarrheal diseases.

Microbiota-based diagnostics in microscopic colitis (MC) remain exploratory, but early sequencing studies suggest that fecal community structure may provide complementary discriminatory information in patients with chronic watery diarrhea. In a small case-control analysis, patients with MC showed a marked reduction in Verrucomicrobia, particularly Akkermansia spp., compared with healthy controls, supporting the concept that mucosa-associated ecological disruption may accompany disease onset ref [8]. Because Akkermansia is linked to mucin turnover and epithelial homeostasis, its depletion is biologically plausible and may reflect altered barrier-microbe interactions relevant to MC pathogenesis ref [8].

At present, however, microbiota findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than diagnostic in routine practice. Reported signals are derived from limited cohorts, may be influenced by age, smoking, diet, medication exposure, and stool consistency, and are not yet sufficiently standardized to distinguish MC reliably from irritable bowel syndrome or other causes of chronic diarrhea. Thus, microbiome profiling is best viewed as a future adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, colonoscopy with systematic biopsies.

The principal diagnostic promise of microbiota research lies in multivariable models that integrate microbial signatures with fecal inflammatory markers, histology, and clinical metadata. If validated in larger longitudinal cohorts, such composite approaches could improve pre-endoscopic triage, identify biologically distinct MC subgroups, and perhaps help predict relapse or therapeutic response. For now, the main contribution of microbiota studies is mechanistic: they broaden the diagnostic framework of MC by linking an otherwise subtle inflammatory disorder to measurable alterations in intestinal ecology ref [8].

Microscopic colitis is classically defined by a discordance between symptoms and endoscopic findings: despite chronic watery, non-bloody diarrhea, conventional colonoscopy usually shows a macroscopically normal or near-normal colonic mucosa. Consequently, visual inspection alone has low diagnostic sensitivity, and the diagnosis depends on histologic assessment of colonic biopsies obtained during endoscopy rather than on characteristic gross mucosal abnormalities ref [9], ref [10].

Although the endoscopic appearance is often unremarkable, subtle nonspecific changes may occasionally be reported, including mild edema, erythema, reduced vascular pattern, or abnormal mucosal texture; in collagenous colitis, mucosal tears or linear lacerations have also been described, albeit infrequently. These findings are neither sufficiently sensitive nor specific to exclude or confirm microscopic colitis, so a normal colonoscopy should not deter biopsy sampling when the clinical suspicion is high ref [9], ref [10].

The diagnostic yield of colonoscopy in suspected microscopic colitis is therefore driven by biopsy strategy. Reviews emphasize that a meaningful proportion of patients investigated for chronic diarrhea are diagnosed only when random colonic biopsies are taken, with reported yields in the range of approximately 10-30% in selected chronic diarrhea cohorts. Because histologic abnormalities may be patchy and can be more prominent proximally, multiple biopsies from different colonic segments, including the right and left colon, are recommended rather than relying on rectosigmoid sampling alone ref [9], ref [10].

Histopathology is the diagnostic cornerstone of microscopic colitis, particularly because endoscopic findings are often normal or only subtly abnormal. The two major clinicopathologic subtypes are collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis, both defined by a chronic inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria, surface epithelial injury, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, but distinguished by the status of the subepithelial collagen plate ref [11], ref [2]. Proper interpretation requires well-oriented biopsies, since tangential sectioning can artifactually exaggerate collagen thickness or obscure epithelial lymphocytosis ref [11].

Collagenous colitis is characterized by a thickened, irregular subepithelial collagen band, conventionally measured at greater than 10 μm, often with entrapped capillaries and inflammatory cells; epithelial detachment and degenerative surface changes are common accompanying features ref [11], ref [3]. Lymphocytic colitis, by contrast, lacks a significantly thickened collagen table and is diagnosed primarily by increased surface intraepithelial lymphocytes, typically at least 20 per 100 epithelial cells, together with chronic lamina propria inflammation ref [11], ref [2]. Because these changes may be patchy, multiple biopsies from different colonic segments improve diagnostic sensitivity.

Beyond the classic forms, incomplete microscopic colitis has been recognized for cases showing typical clinical presentation but histologic abnormalities that fall short of full criteria, such as a collagen band of 5–10 μm or mildly increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. This category is clinically relevant because patients may have symptoms and treatment responses similar to those with definite microscopic colitis ref [11], ref [4]. Histologic overlap can also occur during disease evolution or after therapy, underscoring that subtype assignment should integrate quantitative thresholds with overall morphologic context and clinicopathologic correlation ref [11].

Beyond the defining features used for diagnosis, several tissue-level correlates are being explored to better capture disease activity and subtype biology in microscopic colitis. Histologic studies have highlighted that, in addition to increased intraepithelial lymphocytes or a thickened subepithelial collagen band, active disease may show expanded lamina propria inflammation, epithelial injury, and prominent eosinophilic infiltration or degranulation, particularly in collagenous colitis. These observations suggest that microscopic colitis contains quantifiable inflammatory signals that extend beyond conventional binary diagnostic thresholds and may eventually support activity grading or treatment monitoring ref [3], ref [2].

Among candidate noninvasive biomarkers, fecal inflammatory markers have shown only partial utility. Fecal calprotectin can be elevated in microscopic colitis but has inconsistent sensitivity and specificity, limiting its value as a standalone diagnostic test, especially for distinguishing microscopic colitis from functional diarrhea in individual patients ref [3], ref [3]. By contrast, eosinophil-associated fecal proteins, including eosinophil cationic protein and eosinophil protein X, have been reported to correlate more closely with active collagenous colitis and may reflect the eosinophil-rich mucosal response seen histologically ref [3], ref [4], ref [5].

Overall, the current biomarker landscape remains exploratory rather than practice-changing. Blood-based markers lack specificity, and fecal assays have not yet replaced colonoscopic biopsy for diagnosis or response assessment. The most plausible near-term direction is an integrated model combining routine histopathology with selected inflammatory readouts and possibly molecular tissue signatures, but these approaches still require standardization, validation in larger cohorts, and demonstration of incremental value in routine care ref [3].

subsections.subsection_title: Long-Term Outcomes and Quality of Life under Management
subsections.content:
Long-term follow-up indicates that microscopic colitis (MC) is often a chronic, relapsing disorder rather than a uniformly self-limited condition. In a case–control study with median disease duration of approximately 6 years, patients with collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis continued to report more gastrointestinal and systemic symptoms than matched controls, including abdominal pain, fatigue, nocturnal defecation and fecal incontinence; importantly, several of these differences persisted even among patients classified as being in clinical remission on stool frequency criteria alone, underscoring that symptom control and patient-perceived recovery are not fully synonymous ref [12].

Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) is therefore a central therapeutic outcome. The same long-term study showed significantly impaired Short Health Scale domains in MC compared with controls, particularly in symptom burden and disease-related worry, suggesting that residual symptoms, uncertainty about relapse, and extraintestinal complaints continue to affect daily functioning despite management ref [12]. This observation is clinically relevant because MC also shows substantial diagnostic overlap with functional bowel disorders; a meta-analysis found a high prevalence of functional bowel disorder features in MC, which may contribute to persistent symptoms and reduced quality of life even when inflammatory activity appears quiescent ref [12].

Histologic evolution also supports the need for prolonged follow-up in selected patients. In a large regional cohort, post-diagnostic biopsies demonstrated persistence of histologic abnormalities for up to 1 year in most patients with collagenous colitis and a substantial proportion with lymphocytic colitis, whereas incomplete MC was less persistent ref [8]. Taken together, current evidence suggests that long-term management should assess more than stool frequency alone, incorporating relapse tendency, ongoing symptom burden, continence, fatigue, and HRQoL, with attention to possible coexisting functional symptoms when treatment response appears incomplete ref [12], ref [8], ref [12].

Medication review is a central component of microscopic colitis management because several commonly prescribed agents have been associated with disease onset or exacerbation. In particular, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, proton pump inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and statins have been repeatedly implicated, with the strongest signal reported for current exposure and for concomitant NSAID–PPI use, which appears to confer especially high risk ref [15]. Accordingly, treatment algorithms should include systematic reconciliation of recent and chronic medications, followed by withdrawal or substitution of potentially offending drugs whenever clinically feasible.

These medication-associated considerations are practical rather than merely etiologic: stopping a suspected trigger may reduce ongoing mucosal injury, limit relapse risk, and improve the response to standard anti-inflammatory therapy. Because many patients are older and exposed to polypharmacy, the balance between symptom control and the need for gastroprotection, analgesia, or psychotropic treatment should be individualized. Where drug cessation is not possible, clinicians should at least recognize these exposures as potential contributors to persistent diarrhea and interpret treatment failure in that context ref [15].

Lifestyle counseling also deserves attention, although evidence is less actionable than for medication withdrawal. In a large prospective cohort, no clear associations were found between microscopic colitis and specific macronutrients, fatty acids, fiber, or zinc intake, arguing against routine disease-specific dietary restriction in the absence of patient-identified triggers ref [16]. By contrast, smoking was strongly associated with microscopic colitis, and higher alcohol intake showed a positive trend with risk ref [16]. Therefore, management should emphasize smoking cessation, moderation of alcohol consumption, and supportive individualized dietary advice focused on symptom tolerance, hydration, and avoidance of unnecessary restrictive diets.

subsections.subsection_title: Current Management Strategies and Treatment Overviews
subsections.content:
Current management of microscopic colitis is stepwise and symptom-oriented, with the primary goals of controlling watery diarrhea, improving quality of life, and preventing relapse. Initial management includes withdrawal of potentially triggering medications when feasible, correction of dehydration or electrolyte disturbances, and use of antidiarrheal therapy in mild disease. Across reviews, budesonide remains the best-supported active treatment and is regarded as the preferred first-line therapy for both collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis because it induces rapid clinical remission in a substantial proportion of patients while minimizing systemic corticosteroid exposure ref [10], ref [1].

For patients with mild or intermittent symptoms, loperamide and, in selected cases, bile acid-binding agents may be sufficient, whereas mesalamine and bismuth subsalicylate have shown more variable benefit and generally occupy adjunctive or alternative roles rather than central positions in treatment algorithms ref [10], ref [3]. Systemic corticosteroids can be effective but are usually reserved for exceptional situations because of their less favorable safety profile compared with budesonide. Immunomodulators such as azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, and rarely biologic therapy, have been used in refractory or budesonide-dependent disease, although evidence remains limited and is based largely on small series and expert practice rather than robust trials ref [10], ref [1].

Overall, treatment overviews emphasize that microscopic colitis is usually manageable but often relapsing. Maintenance strategies are therefore individualized, particularly in patients who recur after induction therapy. This practical framework—remove exacerbating factors, treat active disease with budesonide, and escalate selectively in refractory cases—has become the core contemporary management paradigm described across major reviews ref [10], ref [1], ref [3].

subsections.subsection_title: Predictors of Treatment Response and Disease Activity Assessment
subsections.content:
Assessment of treatment response in microscopic colitis remains challenging because symptoms, histology, and inflammatory biomarkers do not consistently move in parallel. Prospective work developing a Microscopic Colitis Disease Activity Index suggests that disease activity is best captured by a symptom-centered framework, with stool frequency, stool consistency, abdominal pain, nocturnal symptoms, and fecal incontinence among the most discriminative variables separating symptomatic from asymptomatic patients ref [18]. In practice, this supports using standardized clinical symptom assessment as the principal tool for monitoring response, while recognizing that histologic remission is less well validated as a routine therapeutic target.

Available evidence indicates that robust baseline predictors of pharmacologic response are limited. In a tertiary-center cohort including both collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis, budesonide showed the highest response rates in both subtypes, whereas response to other therapies was more variable; importantly, histologic subtype itself did not significantly predict differential treatment response ref [17]. The same study identified older age at diagnosis as associated with better response to bismuth subsalicylate, but few other clinical variables reliably stratified outcomes ref [17]. These findings underscore that currently available predictors are modest and insufficient to replace empirical, response-guided treatment selection.

Disease activity assessment should also be distinguished from diagnostic prediction. A validated clinical scoring system has been proposed to identify patients with chronic diarrhea who are more likely to harbor microscopic colitis and therefore warrant colonoscopic biopsy ref [19]. Although this tool is not a treatment-response index, it is relevant to disease activity pathways because earlier case identification may reduce delays in initiating effective therapy. Overall, contemporary management still relies on repeated clinical assessment rather than validated biomarker- or histology-driven algorithms, highlighting an important unmet need for prognostic markers that can predict relapse, steroid responsiveness, and sustained remission ref [17], ref [18].

Guideline-based pharmacologic management of microscopic colitis is primarily symptom-oriented, because the disease is not associated with increased colorectal cancer risk or other adverse long-term inflammatory sequelae; thus, the therapeutic objective is clinical remission with minimal treatment toxicity rather than histologic normalization ref [20], ref [21]. Across both collagenous and lymphocytic colitis, the American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) recommends budesonide as first-line therapy for induction of remission in patients with symptomatic disease, reflecting the most consistent evidence base among available agents ref [20], ref [21].

When budesonide is not feasible, the guideline framework recognizes a step-down hierarchy of less well-supported alternatives. Mesalamine may be considered in selected patients, although it is less effective than budesonide, while bismuth subsalicylate can be used as an alternative in mild disease or when corticosteroid exposure is undesirable ref [20], ref [9]. In contrast, the AGA suggests against combination therapy with cholestyramine plus mesalamine over mesalamine alone, and systemic prednisone/prednisolone is generally reserved for situations in which budesonide cannot be used because of its less favorable safety profile ref [20], ref [21].

For patients with recurrent symptoms after induction, budesonide is also recommended for maintenance of clinical remission, consistent with the high relapse rates observed after drug withdrawal ref [20], ref [21]. Refractory cases may require escalation beyond standard guideline-backed options; thiopurines or biologic therapy have been described in review literature, but supporting evidence remains limited and largely based on uncontrolled experience rather than robust comparative trials ref [21], ref [9]. Overall, current guideline algorithms therefore position budesonide as the cornerstone of pharmacologic care, with alternative and rescue therapies individualized according to contraindications, relapse pattern, and treatment tolerance ref [20], ref [9].
